evidence.claim: A parkway reshaped by wetlands, with a trail beside the traffic.
evidence.quote: The design of the road was re-envisioned to include extensive wetland protection west of the parkway and in the parkway median, a trail system along the side of the parkway

evidence.claim: Legacy Parkway curves along Great Salt Lake wetlands, with nature preserves to the west and rail lines and I-15 to the east.
evidence.quote: Wetlands of the nearby Great Salt Lake and nature preserves border the western side of the parkway while the eastern side roughly parallels Union Pacific and Utah Transit Authority rail lines and I-15.

evidence.claim: Visit Utah highlights lake views and the millions of migrating birds that feed here each spring and fall.
evidence.quote: Millions of migratory birds enjoy Great Salt Lake as a huge cafeteria as they pass through from South America and Canada each spring and fall.

evidence.claim: Utah designated the parkway a state scenic byway in 2002; in 2018, the designation was renamed Great Salt Lake Scenic Byway and extended toward Antelope Island Marina.
evidence.quote: (a) Designated May 16, 2002. (b) Name changed July 19, 2018 to Great Salt Lake Scenic Byway. (c) Extended July 19, 2018

evidence.claim: Construction started in 2001, then stopped amid lawsuits over the environmental review.
evidence.quote: Initial construction of Legacy Parkway began in 2001; however, it was forced to stop as a result of lawsuits over the completeness of the environmental impact statement (EIS).

evidence.claim: A federal appeals court found the review inadequate for failing to study alternative routes less harmful to wetlands.
evidence.quote: as it did not study other alternate routes that were less harmful to wetlands

evidence.claim: A revised review changed the alignment and enlarged Legacy Nature Preserve; Utah and the Sierra Club signed a compromise in 2005.
evidence.quote: A supplemental EIS (SEIS), which changed the routing of the highway as well as increased the amount of land to be part of the Legacy Nature Preserve, was completed in January 2005.

evidence.claim: The road opened in September 2008 as a four-lane parkway instead of the planned six-lane expressway.
evidence.quote: Original plans for the highway had included a six-lane expressway, compared to the four-lane controlled-access parkway that was built.

evidence.claim: Heading south, begin at Farmington’s Wasatch Weave interchange west of Lagoon.
evidence.quote: before terminating at a triple-junction with I-15, SR-225 and U.S. Route 89 west of Lagoon. This interchange is referred to as the Wasatch Weave.

evidence.claim: Continue past Centerville and West Bountiful’s wetland curves, then through Woods Cross toward I-215.
evidence.quote: In West Bountiful, the parkway curves to the northeast as it follows the contour of the wetlands which lie on the western side of the road.

evidence.claim: Legacy Nature Preserve borders the southern stretch, and the Legacy Parkway Trail parallels the entire road.
evidence.quote: For the entirety of the parkway's length it is paralleled by the Legacy Parkway Trail

evidence.claim: Visit Utah highlights lake views
evidence.quote: with views of the world-famous Great Salt Lake.

evidence.claim: extended toward Antelope Island Marina.
evidence.quote: State Route 127 from the Junction with the West Davis Corridor running west or southwest to the Antelope Island Marina.

evidence.claim: Utah and the Sierra Club signed a compromise in 2005.
evidence.quote: On September 21, 2005, the State of Utah and the Sierra Club (acting on behalf of numerous groups opposing the overall Legacy Highway project) officially signed a compromise regarding Legacy Parkway.

evidence.claim: The road opened in September 2008
evidence.quote: Construction began in 2006 and was completed in 2008, with the parkway opening in September of the same year.

evidence.claim: Continue past Centerville and West Bountiful’s wetland curves, then through Woods Cross toward I-215.
evidence.quote: The parkway travels north from Interstate 215 (I-215) in northwestern Salt Lake City to an interchange named the Wasatch Weave in Farmington with two intermediate interchanges providing access to Woods Cross and Centerville.

evidence.claim: Legacy Nature Preserve borders the southern stretch
evidence.quote: The Legacy Nature Preserve lays along the western border of the parkway near its southern terminus.

evidence.claim: The road follows the wetland contours at West Bountiful.
evidence.quote: In West Bountiful, the parkway curves to the northeast as it follows the contour of the wetlands

evidence.claim: Farmington’s Lagoon began with a resort that lost its lakeshore.
evidence.quote: the lake level receded drastically until Lake Park was far from the lake, and the park closed by the end of the 1895 season.

evidence.claim: The Denver & Rio Grande Western Railroad built Lake Park on Great Salt Lake in 1886, but retreating water left it stranded inland.
evidence.quote: In 1886, the Denver & Rio Grande Western Railroad built a resort called Lake Park on the shores of the Great Salt Lake.

evidence.claim: After it closed in 1895, Simon Bamberger bought most of its buildings and moved them about three miles east to attract passengers to his Salt Lake & Ogden Railroad.
evidence.quote: To increase passenger traffic on his line, he bought most of the original Lake Park buildings from the D&RGW and moved them about 3 miles (5 km) east near Farmington, Utah.

evidence.claim: Lagoon opened at Farmington in July 1896.
evidence.quote: Lagoon opened in Farmington on July 12, 1896,

evidence.claim: Its name came from the small body of water on the original forty-acre property.
evidence.quote: The resort was named Lagoon for the small body of water located on the original forty acres

evidence.claim: Centerville occupies a narrow strip between the Wasatch Mountains and Farmington Bay.
evidence.quote: The city is situated on a thin strip of land between the Wasatch Mountain Range and Farmington Bay.

evidence.claim: Its name began as a measurement: an 1850 survey placed the town precisely between Farmington and Bountiful.
evidence.quote: After an 1850 survey found the town was located precisely between Farmington and Bountiful, it became known as Centerville

evidence.claim: Before that, it had been Deuel Settlement and then Cherry Creek, named after the Cherry family.
evidence.quote: The community was originally known as Deuel Settlement but was renamed to Cherry Creek after the Cherry family arrived.

evidence.claim: Shadrach Roundy built a gristmill on Deuel Creek in the winter of 1849 and also used it to make molasses from corn stalks.
evidence.quote: in the winter of 1849 he built a grist mill on Deuel Creek. He also made molasses from corn stalks at this mill.

evidence.claim: The Utah Central Rail Road reached Centerville in 1869.
evidence.quote: In 1869, the Utah Central Rail Road reached Centerville.

evidence.claim: Near the parkway’s southern end, the road forms Legacy Nature Preserve’s eastern boundary.
evidence.quote: The eastern border of the Legacy Nature Preserve is formed by the parkway as it travels north.

evidence.claim: The preserve gained land when a supplemental environmental review changed the highway’s route in 2005.
evidence.quote: A supplemental EIS (SEIS), which changed the routing of the highway as well as increased the amount of land to be part of the Legacy Nature Preserve, was completed in January 2005.

evidence.claim: That review also added the trail system beside the road.
evidence.quote: The SEIS also added in the trail system that now parallels the parkway.

evidence.claim: The redesign protected wetlands west of the pavement and in the median, with pedestrian bridges and underpasses connecting the trail system.
evidence.quote: The design of the road was re-envisioned to include extensive wetland protection west of the parkway and in the parkway median, a trail system along the side of the parkway, and numerous pedestrian overpasses and underpasses for ease of access to the trail system.

evidence.claim: Along the full parkway, protected land totals 2,225 acres to the west, with another 20 acres of wetlands along the highway.
evidence.quote: There are a total of 2,225 acres (900 ha) of protected areas to the west of the highway, and an additional 20 acres (8.1 ha) of wetlands along the length of the highway.

evidence.claim: The settlement initially limited speeds and excluded semi-trucks except in specified circumstances. Those restrictions expired on January 1, 2020, when trucks were allowed and the speed limit rose to 65 mph.
evidence.quote: The compromise agreement restrictions had a sunset date of January 1, 2020, at which time the speed limit was increased to 65 mph (105 km/h) and trucks were no longer banned.

evidence.claim: The settlement initially limited speeds and excluded semi-trucks except in specified circumstances.
evidence.quote: limited the speed on the road and banned semi-trucks on the highway except in emergencies.

evidence.claim: The park added a wooden roller coaster in 1921, designed by John Miller, as rides joined the original music and restaurants.
evidence.quote: Lagoon's wooden coaster, Roller Coaster, was designed by John Miller and constructed in 1921.

evidence.claim: the original music and restaurants.
evidence.quote: Lagoon opened in Farmington on July 12, 1896, and featured live music and restaurants.

evidence.claim: The settlement preceded the name: Thomas Grover arrived in the autumn of 1847, and a log schoolhouse followed in 1851.
evidence.quote: Centerville was first settled by Thomas Grover in the autumn of 1847.

evidence.claim: a log schoolhouse followed in 1851.
evidence.quote: In 1851, a log school house was built in Centerville

evidence.claim: Farther north, the road also forms much of the eastern edge of Farmington Bay Waterfowl Management Area.
evidence.quote: Further north, the parkway forms much of the eastern border of the Farmington Bay Waterfowl Management Area.

flags: This entry follows the original parkway southward to match the strip map. The 2018 designation includes the then-future West Davis Corridor and Antelope Island Marina; designation alone is not evidence of access or completion.
Cached lengths differ: 11.5 miles in the parkway article, 14 miles in Visit Utah and 12.2 mapped miles in material. Omitted mileage and drive time rather than merge scopes.
No unsupported current moment claim was dropped. Clarified that most Lake Park buildings moved, and distinguished the revised environmental review from the later settlement.
The old truck restriction expired January 1, 2020; it is not presented as a current driving restriction. No practical note is needed for this historical account.
Legacy Nature Preserve has no dedicated cached page or coordinates; retained its existing absence of at. The acreage is for the full parkway, not the preserve alone.
